questions.scenario: An interviewer says: 'Design a transfer API for a digital bank.' and waits.
questions.question: What is the best first move?
options: Draw Kafka, Kubernetes and ten microservices
Start writing Java code
Ask which cloud provider the bank uses and stop there
Clarify functional and non-functional requirements (scale, consistency, availability, compliance) and state assumptions
questions.explanation: Requirements and assumptions frame every later choice; interviewers assess this structure.

questions.scenario: A bank expects 4 million transfers per day.
questions.question: Roughly what average request rate is that, and what should you plan for?
options: About 46,000 per second
About 4 per second; peaks don't matter
About 4,000 per second on average
About 46 per second on average; plan for peaks several times higher

questions.scenario: A team proposes caching account balances in Redis for 60 seconds to speed up transfer authorisation.
questions.question: What is the main problem?
options: Redis can't store decimals
60 seconds is too short for any cache
Stale balances could authorise debits that overdraw accounts; balances used for decisions must come from the source of truth under a lock
Caches always slow systems down
questions.explanation: Cache read-mostly data that tolerates staleness, not data used to authorise money movement.

questions.scenario: Statement queries overload the primary database. The team adds an asynchronous read replica for statements.
questions.question: What trade-off must they handle?
options: Replication lag: a customer may not immediately see a transfer they just made, so recent activity may need to come from the primary
Replicas can't run SELECT queries
Replicas remove the need for backups
Replicas double write throughput
questions.explanation: Async replicas can be behind; design for read-your-own-writes where it matters.

questions.scenario: After a transfer, the API calls SMS, email and fraud services synchronously, and an SMS outage makes transfers time out.
questions.question: What design change helps most?
options: Retry the whole transfer when SMS fails
Add a longer timeout to the SMS call
Remove fraud scoring
Commit the transfer, publish an event (via an outbox) to a queue, and let consumers process notifications independently with retries
questions.explanation: Queues decouple slow or failing follow-up work from the critical path.

questions.scenario: Which statements about horizontal scaling of a Spring Boot API are true? (Choose two.)
questions.question: Select two.
options: In-memory locks and rate limits stop working correctly across instances
It automatically scales the database
It removes the need for health checks
Instances should be stateless so any instance can serve any request
questions.explanation: Stateless instances behind a load balancer scale out; shared state and locks must move to shared infrastructure.

questions.scenario: An interviewer asks how your payment hub behaves when a provider times out after possibly charging the customer.
questions.question: What is the strongest answer?
options: Retry the charge until it succeeds
Record the payment as pending, resolve the outcome with status queries or webhooks, and never retry the charge blindly
Ask the customer to try again
Treat every timeout as a failure and refund
questions.explanation: Unknown outcomes need resolution, not guesses; idempotency and status checks prevent double charges.
